                  <ns0:head>CHAP. V.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 I Am come into my garden <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">This is the Bridegrooms Answer to her Request, delivered in the next foregoing words.</ns0:note>, my sister, <ns0:hi>my</ns0:hi> spouse; I have gathered my myrrhe with my spice, I have eaten my honey-comb with my honey, I have drunk my wine with my milk <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">I have eaten of my pleasant fruits, as thou didst desire. I have taken notice of, and delight in the service and Obedience of my People.</ns0:note>: eat, O friends <ns0:hi>c,</ns0:hi> drink, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>and be drunken</ns0:hi> with <ns0:hi>loves.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> yea, drink abundantly, O beloved. <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">The friends of the Bride<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />groom. Whereby he understands either 1. The holy Angels and glorified Saints, who in a sublime and spiritual sense may be said to eat and drink in Heaven, the happiness whereof is frequent<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly represented under the name and notion of a Feast: Or rather 2. Believers or Members of the Church militant upon Earth, who by the Argument of Christs gracious presence with them, and ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceptation of their works signified in the last words, are here invi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted and encouraged with great freedom and chearfulness to eat and drink their spiritual Food, to feed upon Gods Holy Word and Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />craments, to eat the Flesh and drink the Blood of the Son of God, who here gives them, an hearty welcome to this Feast.</ns0:note>
                  </ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 I sleep <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>I was asleep, i. e.</ns0:hi> I was dull, and sluggish, and insensi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble of his kind Expressions, and offers of Grace.</ns0:note>, but my heart waketh <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Yet in my ve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry sleep my thoughts were running upon my Beloved, as is not un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />usual in such cases, which at last awakened me. Thus she implies the conflict which was between the Flesh and the Spirit, and the Spirits Victory in the Combate.</ns0:note>: <ns0:hi>it is</ns0:hi> the voice of my beloved <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Between sleeping and waking I fancied that I heard his voice.</ns0:note> that knocketh <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">By his Word, and Providence, and Spirit, at the door of mine Heart, desirous that I would re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceive him by Faith and Love. Compare <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 3. 20.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>saying,</ns0:hi> Open to me <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Inviting me to accept of his gracious Offers, and to let him into my Soul.</ns0:note>, my sister, my love, my dove, my undefiled <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">This heap of kind compellations signifies Christs sincere and fer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vent Affection to his People, notwithstanding her manifold imper<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fections and infirmities. The title of <ns0:hi>dove</ns0:hi> signifies her Chastity and constant Faithfulness to her Husband, for which Doves are famous. How she is undefiled see on <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 4. 7.</ns0:note>: for my head is filled with dew <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Whilest I wait without thy door. He alludes to the custom of Lovers, which oft and willingly suffer such inconveniencies for their hopes and desires of enjoying their Beloved, and signifies his sufferings for the Churches good.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> my locks with the drops of the night <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">The dew which falls in the end of the night, or towards the morn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, whence it is called <ns0:hi>morning dew,</ns0:hi> Hos. 6. 4.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 I have put off my coat <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">My day-cloaths, as persons use to do when they go to rest.</ns0:note>, how shall I put it on <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">It is inconvenient and troublesom to do it at this time. Thus she tacitly reflects upon the Bridegroom for coming to her so unseaso<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nably, and giving her such disturbance, and puts him off to ano<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther time, and excuseth her non-admission of him by her present indisposition, and the difficulty of the thing required of her.</ns0:note>? I have washed my feet <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Which the Eastern people commonly did when they went to Bed, partly to cool their Feet, and partly to cleanse them from that dust and sweat which they had contracted in the day time by Labour and Travel, as being used to go barefoot.</ns0:note>, how shall I defile them?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 My beloved put in his hand by the hole <ns0:hi>of the door</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">He assayed to open the door. When his Word would not prevail, his Spirit, which is ca<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>led <ns0:hi>the finger of God,</ns0:hi> Luk. 11. 20. compared with <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 12. 28. wrought inwardly upon my Consci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ence, and affected mine heart.</ns0:note>, and my bowels were moved <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, (as some read) <ns0:hi>in me.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> for him <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">With compassion for him and his sufferings, and with affection to him; for both these ways is this Phrase oft used, as <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 37. 1. <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 2. 1, 2. &c.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:561" />5 I rose up to open to my beloved <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">I repented of my former drowsiness and neglect, and went forth to receive him.</ns0:note>, and my hands dropped <ns0:hi>with</ns0:hi> myrrhe <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> With Oil or Ointment made of Myrrhe, which either 1. She had taken out of her own stock to prepare her self for the entertainment of the Bridegroom: Or ra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther 2. Dropped from the Bridegrooms hand upon the door in great abundance, when he <ns0:hi>put it into the <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> of the door,</ns0:hi> v. 4. and con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sequently upon her hands and fingers when she touched the door to open it. By which she signifies that Christ though he with<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />drew himself from her, yet left a sweet savour behind him, in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>using into her, and stir<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ing up in her the Graces of the Spirit, such as Repentance, which is bitter as Myrrhe, earnest desire af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter Christ, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, and my fingers <ns0:hi>with</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>passing,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>running a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bout,</ns0:hi> Nah. 1. 8. <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> sweet smelling myrrhe, upon the handles of the lock <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>with <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> passing</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>flowing upon the handles of the lock,</ns0:hi> which place the Bridegroom had touched when he attempted to open it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 I opened to my beloved, but my beloved had withdrawn himself <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Denied me his gracious and comfortable presence, as a just pu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nishment for my former neglect and <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>olly.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> was gone <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Either she repeats the same thing to shew how deeply she was affected with it: Or this is added to imply that he had not only stepped aside, but was quite gone away.</ns0:note>: my soul failed <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>went out</ns0:hi> of me. I fainted and was ready to die away through excessive passion, as this Phrase is used, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 35. 18. & 42. 28. and elsewhere.</ns0:note> when he spake <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>for what he spoke,</ns0:hi> for those endearing Expressions related <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 2. which then I did not heed, but this sad occasion brings them to my remem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />brance: as oft times that word which is ineffectual when it is preach<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed, is afterwards brought to a mans Mind, and produceth blessed effects.</ns0:note>: I <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 3. 1.</ns0:note> sought him <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">By diligent enquiry and importunate Prayer.</ns0:note>, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">That so he might both chastise her folly, and quicken her desires, and prepare the way for a more hearty welcome, and his longer abode with her.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 The watch-men that went about the city <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The Governours of the Church, as <ns0:hi>Ch.</ns0:hi> 3. 3. who, though by their place and office they be obliged to comfort and protect the faithful, do frequently discourage and oppress them, as they ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nifestly did both in the days of <ns0:hi>Isaiah,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Ieremiah,</ns0:hi> and the other holy Prophets, and in the time of Christ and his Apostles, and in divers other Ages.</ns0:note>, found me, they smote me, they wounded me <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">With bitter Calumnies and Persecutions.</ns0:note>; the keepers of the walls <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">The same with the Watch-men, whose Office it is to keep the Gates and Walls of the City.</ns0:note> took away my vail <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Which was an ornament of her Sex, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 3. 23. and a badge of her Modesty, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 24. 65. or an en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sign of her Relation and Subjection to Christ, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 20. 16. 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 11. 5. And so the taking of this Veil away, signifies their contemp<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tuous and injurious usage of her, their endeavours to blast her Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />putation, and to represent and treat her as a common and impu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dent prostitute, and as one that had no Relation to Christ.</ns0:note> from me.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Of whom see on <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1. 5. & 2. 7. The Church having passed the Watch-men, and patiently born, and in a manner forgotten their injuries, proceeds in the pursuit of her beloved, and enquires of every particular Believer or Professor whom she meets concerning him.</ns0:note>, if ye find my beloved <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> what.</ns0:note> that ye tell him, that I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> sick of love <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">That I am ready to faint for want of his presence, and the tokens of his Favour. Use all your interest and importunity with him on my behalf.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 What <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> thy beloved more than <ns0:hi>another</ns0:hi> beloved <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Wherein doth he excel them? Which Professors of Religion might ask, because they were ignorant of Christs Excellency, and true Believers might ask it, that they might be more fully in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />formed of it, and might give the Spouse occasion to discourse of that subject which was very grateful to them.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 1. 8.</ns0:note> O thou fairest among women <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Whose Beauty may command the Respects and Affections of the most worthy per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sons; and therefore we conclude it must be some person of trans<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cendent excellency with whom thou are so highly enamoured.</ns0:note>? What is thy belo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ved more than <ns0:hi>another</ns0:hi> beloved, that thou dost so charge us?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 My beloved <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> white and ruddy <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Which two colours rightly mixed together, make a Face beau<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tiful. Or the <ns0:hi>white</ns0:hi> may note his pure and spotless Innocency, and the brightness of his Glory and Majesty, and the <ns0:hi>ruddy</ns0:hi> colour may intimate his bloody passion, which made him amiable both to God and Men.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>a stan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dard-bearer.</ns0:hi> or, <ns0:hi>taller than ten thousand.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> the chiefest <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>the standard bearer;</ns0:hi> for such are usually persons of great Eminency, both for Stature, and Courage, and Dignity.</ns0:note> among ten thousand <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Among all persons, Angels or Men. A certain number is put for an uncertain. There are other Kings, and Priests, and Prophets, but none to be compared with him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 His head <ns0:hi>is as</ns0:hi> the most fine gold <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">It shines like Gold, not in respect of the Hair, which is black, as it followeth, but by reason of his Crown of pure Gold upon his Head, <ns0:hi>Rev.</ns0:hi> 14. 14 Whereby she implies that her Bridegroom was a King, which she declared above, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 3. 11.</ns0:note>, his locks <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">In which a part of Mans Beauty consists. I shall not trouble my Reader with a distinct application of this and the following particulars, unto some special part or excellency of Christ, because such things are meer conje<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctures without any solid grounds, and the only design of this de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />scription seems to be this, to set forth the beauty of Christ under the notion of a most compleat and amiable person, in whom there is no defect nor blemish, from the crown of his Head to the sole of his Feet.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> curled.</ns0:note> bushy, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> black as a raven <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Which is mentioned, partly because this was esteem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed a beauty, and partly because it was an evidence of his Youth and vigor, as grey hairs are characters of age and infirmity, <ns0:hi>Hos.</ns0:hi> 7. 9.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 1. 15. & 4. 1.</ns0:note> His eyes <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>the eyes</ns0:hi> of doves <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Lovely and pleasant, chaste and innocent.</ns0:note> by the rivers of waters <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Where they de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />light to abide, and wherewith they bath themselves, and wash their Eyes, where also their Eyes are most lively and beautiful, both by the reflection of the waters, and from that pleasure which they take in such places.</ns0:note>, washed with milk <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Which may belong either 1. To the Eyes, which are supposed to be washed with water, as white and pure as Milk: Or 2. To the Doves, which are intimated to be of a milk-white colour, which in those parts was most esteemed, which colour also made the Eyes appear more lovely.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>sitting in fulness,</ns0:hi> that is, <ns0:hi>fitly placed, & set as a pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cious stone in the soil of a Ring.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> fitly set <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Neither sinking into the Head, nor standing out too much, but in a mode<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rate and comely scituation. Heb. <ns0:hi>sitting in fullness:</ns0:hi> which may note a full and competently large Eye, which is esteemed one beauty of the Eye.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 His cheeks <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">His Face or Countenance, an eminent part whereof is the Cheeks, in which the Beauty or Deformity of a Face doth much consist.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> as a bed <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Which being higher than other parts of the Garden fitly represents the Cheeks, which are higher than other parts of the Face.</ns0:note> of spices <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Not of drie spices, for they are not in Beds, but of Aromatical Flowers which delight both the Eye with a pleasant prospect, and the smell with their fragrancy. This may also signifie the down or hair upon the Bridegrooms cheeks, which is the evi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dence of his mature and vigorous Age, and may denote that Christs sweetness and gentleness is accompanied with Majesty, and Gravi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty, and just severity.</ns0:note>, as <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> towers of perfumes.</ns0:note> sweet flowers <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">This may be added to explain the former Phrase. Or, <ns0:hi>towers of perfumes, i. e.</ns0:hi> Boxes in which perfumes were put, which by their height or form, had some resemblance to a Turret.</ns0:note>: his lips <ns0:hi>like</ns0:hi> lilies <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Beautiful and pleasant. Or this is meant of that sort of Lillies which were of a red or purple colour, as ancient Writers affirm, and so signifie the grateful colour of the Lips. This may note that Grace which was poured into Christs Lips, and which flowed from them in sweet and excellent discourses.</ns0:note>, dropping sweet smelling myrrhe <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Not only graceful to the Eye, as Lillies are, but also fragrant to the smell.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 His hands <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The instruments of Action and of Distribution, which may design the actions of Christ and particularly his distributing Gifts and Graces to his Members.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>are as</ns0:hi> gold-rings set with the be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ryll <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Beautiful, and precious, and richly adorned, as it were with Gold-Rings set with precious stones.</ns0:note>: his belly <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Which seems to be here used, either 1. Metonimically, for the Bowels which are contained in the Belly: Or rather 2. Synec<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dochically, for the whole Body, reaching from the neck to the bot<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tom of the Belly, which is distinguished from the Face, and the joints, which are described in the other clauses. For he speaks here of those parts which are visible to the Eye. And thus here is a compleat description of Christs beauty in all parts from his Head to his Feet.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is as</ns0:hi> bright ivory overlaid <ns0:hi>with</ns0:hi> Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phires <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Of a pure and bright white colour, intermixt with blew veins; for some Saphires are of a bright blew colour.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 His legs <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">The instruments of local motion, and the supporters of the bo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dy.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>are as</ns0:hi> pillars of marble <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">White, and streight, and well shaped, and strong. Which may note the firmness and stability of Christs Kingdom in spight of all opposition.</ns0:note>, set upon sockets of fine gold <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Which add both beauty and strength to them. These may note his Feet compared to Gold, either for their great price and worth, or for their singular brightness, for which they are compared to <ns0:hi>fine-brass, Rev.</ns0:hi> 1. 15. or, as others, for his golden shoes wherewith they were covered or adorned, as the Spouse is com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mended from her shoes, <ns0:hi>Cant.</ns0:hi> 7. 1.</ns0:note>: his countenance <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>his aspect</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>appearance,</ns0:hi> his form or Person, as this Hebrew word is elsewhere used.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is as</ns0:hi> Leba<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />non <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">In respect of its Cedars, as the next words explain it, to wit, tall, and upright, and stately, and withal pleasant to the Eye.</ns0:note>, excellent as the cedars.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> his pa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />late.</ns0:note> His mouth <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> ‖ most sweet <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Which was said before in other words, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 13. and is here justly repeated, because it was a principal part of Christs beauty, and the chief instrument of the Spouses Comfort and Happiness, which wholly depends upon his sweet and excellent Speeches, his holy Precepts, and gracious Offers and Promises contained in the Gospel.</ns0:note>, yea, he is altoge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> desires.</ns0:note> lovely <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Not to run out into more particulars, in one word there is no part of him which is not exquisitely beautiful.</ns0:note>. This <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> my beloved, and this <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> my<ns0:note place="margin">† Heb. <ns0:hi>sweet<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> friend, O daughters of Jerusalem <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">And therefore you have no cause to wonder or to blame me if I am transported with Love to so excellent a personage.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
